candidates.statement: To get an idea of the classical theory for linear differential equations one should look at the survey [@Varadarajan] by V.
In the same way, the many regularity properties of the homological equation $X(qz)A(z)-B(z)X(z)=Y(z)$ should retain some particular attention and be clarified in the language of functional analysis.
Last, the $q$-Gevrey filtration should be translated in terms of factorisation of Stokes operators, like in [@MLR].\

We shall use heavily the theta function of Jacobi defined by the following equality: $$\theta_{q}(z) = \sum_{n \in {\mathbf Z}} q^{-n(n+1)/2} z^{n}.$$ This function is holomorphic in ${\mathbf C}^{*}$ with simple zeroes, all located on the discrete $q$-spiral $[-1;q]$, where we write $[a;q] = a q^{{\mathbf Z}} \;,\; (a \in {\mathbf C}^{*})$.

We shall also use its multiplicative translates $\theta_{q,c}(z) = \theta_{q}(z/c)$ (for $c \in {\mathbf C}^{*}$); the function $\theta_{q,c}$ is holomorphic in ${\mathbf C}^{*}$ with simple zeroes, all located on the discrete $q$-spiral $[-c;q]$ and satisfies the functional equation: $\sigma_q\theta_{q,c} = \frac{z}{c} \theta_{q,c}$.\ As is customary for congruence classes, we shall write $\overline{a} = a \pmod{q^{{\mathbf Z}}}$ for the image of $a \in {\mathbf C}^{*}$ in the elliptic curve ${\mathbf{E}_{q}}$.

Then, for a divisor $D = \sum n_{i} [\alpha_{i}]$ over ${\mathbf{E}_{q}}$ (*i.e.*, the $n_{i} \in {\mathbf Z}$, the $\alpha_{i} \in {\mathbf{E}_{q}}$), we shall write $ev_{{\mathbf{E}_{q}}}(D) = \sum n_{i} \alpha_{i} \in {\mathbf{E}_{q}}$ for its evaluation, computed with the group law on ${\mathbf{E}_{q}}$.\ Let $K$ denote any one of the forementioned fields of functions.
We shall call pure such a bundle.\ Direct sums of pure modules play a special role in [@JSFIL], [@RSZ] and in the present paper.

We shall call them tamely irregular, in an intended analogy with tamely ramified extensions in algebraic number theory: for us, they are irregular objects without wild monodromy, as follows from [@RSZ].

We also introduce notational conventions which will be used all along this paper for a module $M$ in ${\mathcal{E}}_{1}^{(0)}$ and its associated graded module $M_{0} = gr(M)$, an object of ${\mathcal{E}}_{mi,1}^{(0)}$.\ The module $M$ may be given the shape $M = ({{\mathbf C}(\{z\})}^{n},\Phi_{A})$, with: $$\label{equation:forme-canonique} A = A_{U} \underset{def}{=} \begin{pmatrix} z^{- \mu_{1}} A_{1} & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & U_{i,j} & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & 0 & \ldots & z^{- \mu_{k}} A_{k} \end{pmatrix},$$ where $\mu_{1} > \cdots > \mu_{k}$ are integers, $r_{i} \in {\mathbf N}^{*}$, $A_{i} \in GL_{r_{i}}({\mathbf C})$ ($i = 1,\ldots,k$) and $$U = (U_{i,j})_{1 \leq i < j \leq k} \in \underset{1 \leq i < j \leq k}{\prod} {\text{Mat}}_{r_{i},r_{j}}({{\mathbf C}(\{z\})}).$$ The associated graded module is then a direct sum $M_{0} = P_{1} \oplus \cdots \oplus P_{k}$, where, for $1 \leq i < j \leq k$, the module $P_{i}$ is pure of rank $r_{i}$ and slope $\mu_{i}$ and can be put into the form $P_{i} = ({{\mathbf C}(\{z\})}^{r_{i}},\Phi_{z^{-\mu_{i} A_{i}}})$.
The definitions here should be compared to those in [@Varadarajan], p.

We shall write ${\mathcal{F}}(M_{0})$ for the set of equivalence classes of pairs $(M,g)$ of a module $M$ and an isomorphismism $g : {\text{gr}}(M) \rightarrow M_{0}$, where $(M,g)$ is said to be equivalent to $(M',g')$ if there exists a morphism $u : M \rightarrow M'$ such that $g = g' \circ {\text{gr}}(u)$ ($u$ is automatically an isomorphism). :::

We write ${\mathfrak{G}}$ for the algebraic subgroup of $GL_{n}$ made up of matrices of the form: $$\label{equation:automorphisme} F = \begin{pmatrix} I_{r_{1}} & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & F_{i,j} & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & 0 & \ldots & I_{r_{k}} \end{pmatrix}.$$ Its Lie algebra ${\mathfrak{g}}$ consists in matrices of the form: $$\label{equation:endomorphisme} f = \begin{pmatrix} 0_{r_{1}} & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & f_{i,j} & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & 0 & \ldots & 0_{r_{k}} \end{pmatrix}.$$ For $F$ in ${\mathfrak{G}}$, we shall write $F[A] = \left(\sigma_qF\right) A F^{-1}$ for the result of the gauge transformation $F$ on the matrix $A$.\ We shall identify $P_{i}$ with $({{\mathbf C}(\{z\})}^{r_{i}},\Phi_{z^{-\mu_{i}} A_{i}})$, where $A_{i} \in GL_{r_{i}}({\mathbf C})$.
In order to illustrate the possible strategies, we shall end this section by examining a specific example.
We shall try, as far as possible, to mimic the methods and the terminology of the "classical" theory (Stokes operators for linear differential equations and summation in sectors along directions).

If one moreover requires $F$ to be compatible with the graduation, that is, to have the form $F = \begin{pmatrix} 1 & f \\ 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix}$, then there is unicity of the formal series $f$, which must satisfy the functional equation: $$f(z) = - u(z) + z f(qz).$$ We call $\hat{f}_{u}$ this unique formal solution (it can be computed by iterating the above fixpoint equation) and $\hat{F}_{u}$ the corresponding formal gauge transformation.

We compare their Laurent series coefficientwise and get: $$\forall n \in {\mathbf Z}\;,\; (1 - \lambda q^{n}) g_{n} = v_{n}.$$ If $\lambda\not\in [1;q]$ (prohibited direction of summation), there is a unique solution $g \in {\mathcal{O}({\mathbf C}^{*},0)}$ (it does converge where it should), thus a unique solution $f \in {\mathcal{M}({\mathbf C}^{*},0)}$ such that $\theta_{q,\lambda} f$ has no poles in ${\mathbf C}^{*}$.
In the next chapter, I shall exhibit an algebraic variant of this construction.
We shall use here the following simple terminology and facts.\ We start from a proper germ of $q^{-{\mathbf N}}$ invariant subset $U$ of $({\mathbf C}^{*},0)$.

Standing alone, this statement confirms our earlier contention in section [0.1](#subsection:devissage){reference-type="ref" reference="subsection:devissage"}, to the effect that all objects of ${\mathcal{E}}_{1}^{(0)}$ are locally equivalent to objects of ${\mathcal{E}}$.\ Now, we shall have use for an extension of these results allowing for coefficients in ${\mathcal{O}({\mathbf C}^{*},0)}$ (instead of ${{\mathbf C}(\{z\})}$).

From the computations in example [\[example:exemple-classique\]](#example:exemple-classique){reference-type="ref" reference="example:exemple-classique"}, we deduce that we have to take $\nu = {\mathcal{B}}_{q,1} u (1) = \sum_{n \in {\mathbf Z}} q^{-n(n-1)/2} u_{n}$; we must then prove the existence and unicity of $f$.

Then: $$\left|f_{n}\right| \leq \frac{C A^{n+1}}{\left|q\right|^{n}} \left( 1 + \frac{A}{\left|q\right|^{n+1}} + \frac{A^{2}}{\left|q\right|^{(n+1) + (n+2)}} + \cdots \right),$$ whence $\left|f_{n}\right| = \text{O}\left( \left(\frac{A}{\left|q\right|}\right)^{n} \right)$ when $n \to + \infty$.\ On the side of negative powers, putting, for convenience, $g_{n} = f_{-n}$ and $v_{k} = u_{-k}$ and, using the second definition for $f'_{n}$, we see that $$g_{n} = q^{n(n+1)/2} \sum_{k = n}^{+ \infty} \frac{v_{k}}{q^{k(k+1)/2}}.$$ By assumption on $u$, we have, for *any* $B > 0$, $\left|v_{k}\right| = \text{O}(B^{k})$ when $k \to + \infty$ and a similar computation as before then yields that, for *any* $B > 0$, $\left|g_{n}\right| = \text{O}(B^{n})$ when $n \to + \infty$, allowing one to conclude that $f \in {\mathcal{O}({\mathbf C}^{*},0)}$ as desired. $\Box$\ We shall actually need only the following consequence of the proposition.
Also, we shall, for $1 \leq i < j \leq k$, use the abreviation: $\mu_{i,j} = \mu_{i} - \mu_{j} \in {\mathbf N}^{*}$.

For a family of recangular blocks $U'_{I,j}$, we shall use the following abreviation: $$A'_{U'} = \begin{pmatrix} A'_{1} & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & U'_{i,j} & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ \ldots & 0 & \ldots & \ldots & \ldots \\ 0 & \ldots & 0 & \ldots & A'_{k} \end{pmatrix},$$

The computations are immediate. $\Box$\ We shall now take two matrices $A_{U}$ and $A_{V}$ in the formal class of $A_{0}$, flatten their slopes through the gauge transformation $\Theta_{D}$, and then link the resulting matrices $A'_{U'}$ and $A'_{V'}$ by an isomorphism defined over ${\mathbf C}^{*}$.

Since $div_{{\mathbf{E}_{q}}}(t_{i}) - div_{{\mathbf{E}_{q}}}(t_{j}) = D_{i,j}$, this proves (and explains) the given condition. $\Box$\ As a matter of notation, we shall write $F_{D}(U,V)$ for the $F$ obtained in the theorem: it does indeed depend solely on $D$.

We shall write in particular $F_{D}(U) = F_{D}(0,U)$.\ Let us call ${\mathfrak{G}}_{D}({\mathcal{M}({\mathbf C}^{*},0)})$ (resp. ${\mathfrak{G}}_{D}({\mathcal{M}({\mathbf C}^{*})})$) the subset of ${\mathfrak{G}}({\mathcal{M}({\mathbf C}^{*},0)})$ (resp. of ${\mathfrak{G}}({\mathcal{M}({\mathbf C}^{*})})$) defined by the constraints: for $1 \leq i < j \leq k$, $\text{div}_{{\mathbf{E}_{q}}}(F_{i,j}) \geq - D_{i,j}$.
